sectionTitle: Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic

specStatements.text: There are three types of strong chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic. For ionic bonding the particles are oppositely charged ions. For covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. For metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons.
Ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.
Students should be able to explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and the transfer or sharing of electrons.

When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred. Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions. Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negatively charged ions. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0).
The electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound can be represented by a dot and cross diagram, eg for sodium chloride
Students should be able to draw dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds formed by metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.
The charge on the ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 relates to the group number of the element in the periodic table.
Students should be able to work out the charge on the ions of metals and non-metals from the group number of the element, limited to the metals in Groups 1 and 2, and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.

An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These forces act in all directions in the lattice and this is called ionic bonding.

Students should be able to:
deduce that a compound is ionic from a diagram of its structure in one of the specified forms
describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent a giant ionic structure
work out the empirical formula of an ionic compound from a given model or diagram that shows the ions in the structure.
Students should be familiar with the structure of sodium chloride but do not need to know the structures of other ionic compounds.
When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds. These bonds between atoms are strong.
Covalently bonded substances may consist of small molecules.
Students should be able to recognise common substances that consist of small molecules from their chemical formula.
Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers.
Some covalently bonded substances have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide.

Students should be able to:
draw dot and cross diagrams for the molecules of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane
represent the covalent bonds in small molecules, in the repeating units of polymers and in part of giant covalent structures, using a line to represent a single bond
describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent molecules or giant structures
deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a given model or diagram in these forms showing the atoms and bonds in the molecule.
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.

The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure. The sharing of delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds. The bonding in metals may be represented in the following form:

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be familiar with the structure of sodium chloride but do not need to know the structures of other ionic compounds.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Sodium chloride is the only ionic structure taught in this file. Every description of a giant ionic lattice, and every question that asks a student to picture how ions are arranged, uses sodium chloride. Other ionic compounds appear only where the specification separately permits them: as charges deduced from group number (4.2.1.2), as dot and cross diagrams of Group 1 or 2 metals with Group 6 or 7 non-metals (4.2.1.2), or as an empirical formula counted from a model that the question itself supplies (4.2.1.3). No question requires recall of the structure of magnesium oxide, calcium fluoride or any other ionic compound.

scopeNotes.statement: limited to the metals in Groups 1 and 2, and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every item that asks a student to work out an ionic charge from a group number uses only Group 1, Group 2, Group 6 or Group 7 elements. Transition metals, Group 3 to 5 elements and variable oxidation states are never used as the basis of a charge deduction, and no question asks for the charge on an iron, copper or lead ion.

scopeNotes.statement: for ionic compounds formed by metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Dot and cross items are restricted to sodium chloride, magnesium chloride, magnesium oxide, lithium fluoride, potassium oxide and calcium fluoride - all Group 1 or 2 metals with Group 6 or 7 non-metals. No dot and cross diagram of a transition metal compound, a polyatomic ion or a non-metal oxide such as aluminium oxide is asked for.

scopeNotes.statement: the molecules of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Dot and cross questions for covalent molecules use only the eight molecules named in the specification. Where another covalent substance appears (poly(ethene), ethene, diamond, silicon dioxide) it is used for a different skill - recognising a large molecule, a giant structure, or reading a formula from a supplied model - never for drawing or interpreting a dot and cross diagram of it.

concepts.definition: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. All three are electrostatic in origin, but they differ in which particles are held together and in what happens to the outer electrons.
Bonding in which the particles are oppositely charged ions. It occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. It occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons. It occurs in metallic elements and in alloys.

The force of attraction between opposite electric charges. Chemical bonding is explained by electrostatic attraction: between positive and negative ions, between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons, or between metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
The movement of electrons from the outer shell of a metal atom to the outer shell of a non-metal atom when the two react. Transfer produces ions; it is not itself the bond.
An ion formed when a metal atom loses one or more electrons from its outer shell. It has more protons than electrons, so its charge is positive.
An ion formed when a non-metal atom gains one or more electrons into its outer shell. It has more electrons than protons, so its charge is negative.
The full outer shell arrangement of a Group 0 element. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
A diagram that shows the electron transfer forming an ionic compound, using dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for the other, so that the origin of each electron can be followed.
For the elements in scope, the charge on the ion follows from the group number: Group 1 forms 1+, Group 2 forms 2+, Group 6 forms 2- and Group 7 forms 1-.
An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions, held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. There are no separate molecules in it.
In an ionic lattice the electrostatic forces act in all directions, not along a fixed line between two chosen ions. This is what is meant by ionic bonding.
The structure of sodium chloride can be shown as a two-dimensional diagram, as a three-dimensional ball and stick model or as a space-filling model. Each is a model of the same giant lattice.

concepts.term: Empirical formula of an ionic compound
concepts.definition: The simplest whole number ratio of the ions in the structure. It is worked out from a model or diagram by counting the ions of each type and cancelling to the simplest ratio.

A ball and stick model shows gaps between ions that do not exist and sticks that are not real; a two-dimensional diagram shows forces in only two directions; no diagram can show the full extent of the lattice.

When atoms share pairs of electrons they form covalent bonds, and these bonds between atoms are strong. The strength of the bonds inside a molecule says nothing about the melting or boiling point of the substance.
A covalently bonded substance may consist of small molecules, each containing a small fixed number of non-metal atoms, such as H2, Cl2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2.
A covalently bonded substance whose molecules are very large: many small molecules joined into long chains. A polymer has very large molecules, not a giant structure.
A structure in which very many atoms are joined by covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, with no separate molecules. Diamond and silicon dioxide are the specification's examples.

concepts.term: Dot and cross diagram of a molecule
concepts.definition: A diagram showing the shared pairs of electrons in a molecule, using dots and crosses to show which atom each electron came from. Required for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane.
A polymer is represented by its repeating unit drawn in brackets with a subscript n, where n is a large number. It is not a value to be calculated from the diagram.
In a displayed formula or a diagram of a giant structure, one line between two atoms represents one single covalent bond, that is one shared pair of electrons.
A dot and cross diagram shows the electrons but not the shape or size; a two-dimensional diagram flattens a three-dimensional molecule; a ball and stick model exaggerates the space between atoms.
The molecular formula is deduced by counting the atoms of each element shown in the model or diagram. The bonds, sticks or lines are not counted, and the number is not reduced to the simplest ratio.
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.

An electron from the outer shell of a metal atom that is no longer held by one atom and is free to move through the whole structure. Sharing these delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
A mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements. The bonding in an alloy is metallic, as it is in a pure metallic element.

misconceptions.question: Is every compound made from two elements an ionic compound?
misconceptions.correct: Ionic bonding occurs only in compounds formed from a metal combined with a non-metal. A compound of two non-metals, such as carbon dioxide, is covalent.
misconceptions.misconception: Any compound built from two different elements must have swapped electrons, so it must be ionic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionic bonding is taught first and is often introduced simply as what happens when two elements combine. The outcome - a compound - sticks, while the condition that one element must be a metal is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Check the periodic table first. Metal plus non-metal gives ionic bonding; non-metal plus non-metal gives covalent bonding.

misconceptions.question: Can a substance made of only one element have covalent bonds?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements, such as hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen and nitrogen, as well as in compounds of non-metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Bonding only happens when two different elements join, so a cylinder of chlorine gas contains no bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bonding is introduced through reactions, so students associate a bond with a chemical change between different elements and never look inside an element.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine gas is Cl2: two atoms sharing a pair of electrons, a covalent bond. The two atoms being the same makes no difference.

misconceptions.question: Brass is copper and zinc. Is the bonding in brass ionic?
misconceptions.correct: No. Brass is an alloy, and metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.
misconceptions.misconception: Brass contains two different elements, so one must have given electrons to the other, making it ionic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule metal plus non-metal is remembered as two elements combined, so any two-element substance is filed as ionic.
misconceptions.correction: Both copper and zinc are metals. Neither will accept electrons, so no ions form. The atoms share delocalised electrons - metallic bonding.

misconceptions.question: Are electrons shared in ionic bonding?
misconceptions.correct: No. In ionic bonding electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom. Sharing is what happens in covalent and metallic bonding.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms share electrons in every kind of bonding; in ionic bonding they just share unequally.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase sharing electrons is used so often as a general description of bonding that it is applied to all three types.
misconceptions.correction: Sort the three types by what happens to the outer electrons: ionic transfers them, covalent shares pairs between two atoms, metallic shares delocalised electrons across the whole structure.

misconceptions.question: Is the ionic bond the electron that moves across?
misconceptions.correct: No. The bond is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between the oppositely charged ions that the transfer produces.
misconceptions.misconception: The bond is the electron jumping from one atom to the other, so the arrow in the diagram is the bond.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dot and cross diagrams draw an arrow for the transfer, and the arrow is the most eye-catching feature, so it is read as the bond itself.
misconceptions.correction: The transfer happens once and is over; what remains is a positive ion and a negative ion attracting each other. That attraction is the bond.

misconceptions.question: Sodium has one outer electron. Does it gain seven electrons?
misconceptions.correct: No. It loses its single outer electron to become Na+ with the electronic structure of neon.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom needs eight outer electrons, so sodium gains seven to fill its outer shell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule full outer shell is remembered without the second half - the easiest route to a full shell. Emptying a nearly empty shell is not considered.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the routes: gaining seven electrons or losing one. Losing one is far easier, and the shell below is already full, so Na+ is 2,8.

misconceptions.question: A magnesium atom loses two electrons. Is the ion negative?
misconceptions.correct: No. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is Mg2+, positively charged.
misconceptions.misconception: Losing something makes you go down, so losing electrons should give a negative charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Loss is associated with less and with minus signs, and the charge that is actually lost is negative, so the signs get crossed.
misconceptions.correction: Count the charges. Magnesium has 12 protons and 12 electrons. Remove two electrons and 12 positives face 10 negatives, so the ion is 2+.

misconceptions.question: Is the charge on a Group 6 ion equal to 6-?
misconceptions.correct: No. A Group 6 atom gains two electrons to reach a full outer shell, so the ion is 2-.
misconceptions.misconception: The charge is just the group number, so Group 6 gives 6- and Group 7 gives 7-.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Group number is correctly linked to charge for Groups 1 and 2, where the two numbers happen to be equal, and the rule is then carried straight across to Groups 6 and 7.
misconceptions.correction: For Groups 6 and 7 the charge is the number of electrons still needed: 8 minus the group number. Group 6 gains 2, Group 7 gains 1.

misconceptions.question: Does a magnesium ion have the same electronic structure as a magnesium atom?
misconceptions.correct: No. The atom is 2,8,2 and the ion is 2,8 - the outer electrons have gone.
misconceptions.misconception: It is still magnesium, so the electron arrangement written down must stay the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electronic structure is learned as a property of the element, tied to its place in the periodic table, so it is treated as fixed.
misconceptions.correction: The element is set by the number of protons, which never changes. The electrons do change, and that is the whole point of ion formation.

misconceptions.question: In a dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride, does Na+ keep an outer electron?
misconceptions.correct: No. The transferred electron is drawn in the chlorine outer shell, so the sodium ion is shown with an empty outer shell and a 1+ charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium still has that electron somewhere, so it should be drawn in the sodium ion as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The electron is drawn as a cross and can be seen on the chloride side, but students copy the atom diagram out of habit and leave the electron in place on both sides.
misconceptions.correction: An electron drawn twice would be two electrons. Draw it once, in the shell it moved to, and put the charges on the brackets.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium is 2+ and chloride is 1-. Is the formula MgCl?
misconceptions.correct: No. Two chloride ions are needed to balance one magnesium ion, so the compound is MgCl2.
misconceptions.misconception: One ion of each pairs up, so magnesium chloride is MgCl.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium chloride is met first, where one to one works, so pairing one ion with one ion becomes the default.
misconceptions.correction: The total positive charge must cancel the total negative charge. One 2+ needs two 1- ions.

misconceptions.question: Does the formula NaCl mean one sodium ion is bonded to one chloride ion?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sodium chloride is a giant structure of ions; NaCl is the simplest ratio, not a molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: NaCl means a pair of ions stuck together, so a crystal is a heap of separate NaCl units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae for small molecules such as H2O are met first and do describe one molecule, so the same reading is applied to an ionic formula.
misconceptions.correction: Each sodium ion in the lattice is attracted to six chloride ions and vice versa. No ion has one partner, so no NaCl molecule exists.

misconceptions.question: A model shows 14 sodium ions and 13 chloride ions. Is the formula Na14Cl13?
misconceptions.correct: No. The empirical formula is NaCl - the simplest whole number ratio, taken from a model that cuts through the lattice unevenly.
misconceptions.misconception: You write down exactly what you counted, so the formula is Na14Cl13.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting atoms works for molecules, where the count is the formula, so the same counting is carried over to a fragment of a lattice.
misconceptions.correction: A lattice has no fixed size, so the count depends on where the model stops. Reduce the numbers to the simplest ratio.

misconceptions.question: Do the gaps in a ball and stick model of sodium chloride really exist?
misconceptions.correct: No. The ions in a real lattice touch; the gaps and sticks are there only to let you see the arrangement.
misconceptions.misconception: The model is a picture of the real thing, so there must be space between the ions with sticks holding them apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Models are handled as physical objects and photographed in textbooks, so their features are taken to be features of the substance.
misconceptions.correction: Treat every model as showing one thing well and other things badly. Ball and stick shows the arrangement; a space-filling model shows how the ions actually pack.

misconceptions.question: Water boils at 100 degrees C. Are the covalent bonds in water weak?
misconceptions.correct: No. The covalent bonds between atoms in a molecule are strong. Boiling separates molecules from each other, not the atoms within them.
misconceptions.misconception: Small molecular substances melt and boil easily, so the covalent bonds holding them must be weak.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One number, the boiling point, is used to judge every force present, because the difference between forces inside a molecule and forces between molecules has not yet been drawn.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what is being pulled apart. Boiling pulls whole molecules apart from one another; the H-O bonds inside each molecule survive intact.

misconceptions.question: Poly(ethene) contains thousands of atoms. Is it a giant covalent structure?
misconceptions.correct: No. Poly(ethene) has very large molecules. Each chain is a separate molecule, unlike diamond where the bonding runs through the whole structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything with thousands of atoms bonded together must be giant covalent like diamond.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Large is treated as the definition of giant, and the difference between a very large molecule and a structure with no molecules at all is a fine one.
misconceptions.correction: Ask whether the substance can be divided into separate molecules. A polymer can - into chains. Diamond cannot.

misconceptions.question: Silicon dioxide has the formula SiO2. Is it a small molecule like CO2?
misconceptions.correct: No. Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure, even though its formula looks like that of carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: SiO2 looks just like CO2, so silicon dioxide must be made of small molecules too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae are used as the main clue to structure, and these two look identical, so the same structure is assumed.
misconceptions.correction: SiO2 is an empirical formula for a giant structure, not a molecule. The specification names silicon dioxide as a giant covalent structure.

misconceptions.question: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in an oxygen molecule?
misconceptions.correct: Two. Each oxygen atom shares two of its outer electrons, giving a double bond - two shared pairs.
misconceptions.misconception: A covalent bond means one shared pair, so O2 and N2 have one shared pair each.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition of a covalent bond as a shared pair is learned from hydrogen and hydrogen chloride, where one pair is all there is.
misconceptions.correction: Count what each atom still needs. Oxygen needs two more electrons, so it must share two pairs; nitrogen needs three, so it shares three.

misconceptions.question: In a displayed formula, does one line represent one electron?
misconceptions.correct: No. One line represents one single covalent bond, which is one shared pair - two electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: The line stands for one electron, so a molecule drawn with four lines has four electrons in its bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A line looks like a single item, and dot and cross diagrams show individual electrons, so the line is matched to one electron rather than to a pair.
misconceptions.correction: Convert between the two pictures: every line in a displayed formula is a pair of electrons in the dot and cross diagram.

misconceptions.question: In the polymer representation, what is n?
misconceptions.correct: n is simply a large number - it shows that the repeating unit is repeated very many times.
misconceptions.misconception: n is a number you have to work out from the diagram, like counting the carbon atoms in the unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other letter in a formula stands for a value that can be found, so n is treated as an unknown to be calculated.
misconceptions.correction: Polymer chains vary in length even within one sample, so there is no single value of n. The specification states only that n is a large number.

misconceptions.question: Does each metal atom keep hold of its own outer electrons?
misconceptions.correct: No. The outer electrons are delocalised and free to move through the whole structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Each atom keeps its own outer electrons but holds them loosely enough to pass them along.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Shell diagrams always show electrons belonging to one atom, and that picture is kept when metals are met.
misconceptions.correction: Delocalised means no longer belonging to any one atom. The electrons form a sea that all the metal ions sit in.

misconceptions.question: Is metallic bonding a kind of ionic bonding?
misconceptions.correct: No. Metallic bonding is the sharing of delocalised electrons between metal atoms; there are no negative ions and no electron transfer between two elements.
misconceptions.misconception: The diagram of a metal shows plus signs and loose electrons, so it must be positive ions attracting negative ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The plus signs in the standard diagram are read as evidence of ionic bonding, since that is the only place plus signs have been seen before.
misconceptions.correction: Ionic bonding needs a non-metal to take the electrons. In a metal nothing takes them - they are shared by every atom at once.

misconceptions.question: When reading a formula from a ball and stick model, do you count the sticks?
misconceptions.correct: No. The formula comes from counting the balls, which are the atoms. The sticks show the bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: Every stick joins something on, so the sticks should be counted as part of the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sticks are the most obvious feature of the model and are the same colour as nothing else, so they are read as another kind of particle.
misconceptions.correction: Count only the balls, sorting them by element, then write the symbols with the counts as subscripts.

misconceptions.question: Does a short two-element formula mean the substance is made of small molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. NaCl and SiO2 have short formulae but are giant structures. Only compounds of non-metals form small molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: A short formula with two symbols in it means a small molecule, so NaCl must be a molecule and hydrogen chloride must be ionic because its name ends in -ide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formula length and the -ide ending are surface features that are quicker to use than checking whether each element is a metal or a non-metal.
misconceptions.correction: Look up each element. Sodium is a metal, so NaCl is ionic and giant. Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so HCl is a small covalent molecule despite its name.

misconceptions.question: In an ionic lattice, do the forces act only between paired ions?
misconceptions.correct: No. The forces act in all directions in the lattice, which is why the whole structure is held together.
misconceptions.misconception: Bonds are lines between two particles, so each ion is bonded along fixed directions to its own partners.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stick in a ball and stick model, and the line in a displayed formula, both show bonding as a link between exactly two particles.
misconceptions.correction: Electrostatic attraction is not a line. A positive ion attracts every negative ion around it, in every direction, throughout the lattice.

misconceptions.question: In the dot and cross diagram of hydrogen, how many bonds are shown?
misconceptions.correct: One. The two electrons in the overlap - one dot and one cross - are a single shared pair, so one covalent bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Each atom puts in an electron and each of those electrons is a bond, so there are two bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two symbols in the overlap look like two separate things, and the phrase each atom contributes an electron encourages counting them one at a time.
misconceptions.correction: Count pairs, not electrons. Two electrons in the overlap make one shared pair, which is one covalent bond.

misconceptions.question: A model of ethene shows two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms. Is the formula CH2?
misconceptions.correct: No. The molecular formula is C2H4, the actual number of atoms in the molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: Formulae should always be written in the simplest form, so C2H4 should be reduced to CH2.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule about simplest whole number ratios is learned for empirical formulae of giant structures and is then applied to molecules as well.
misconceptions.correction: Molecules have a definite number of atoms, so the molecular formula records that number. Simplifying is only for empirical formulae.

misconceptions.question: Are the atoms in a metal arranged randomly?
misconceptions.correct: No. Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals are shiny and can be bent into any shape, so the atoms inside must be jumbled up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word delocalised, and the idea of electrons moving freely, is extended from the electrons to the metal ions themselves.
misconceptions.correction: The ions stay in a regular pattern; only the delocalised electrons move. That regular pattern is why metals form crystals.

misconceptions.question: Are all of the electrons in a metal delocalised?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the electrons in the outer shell of the metal atoms are delocalised.
misconceptions.misconception: The whole atom breaks up in a metal, so every electron it has joins the sea.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sea of electrons picture is drawn without any inner shells, so the remaining positive particles look like bare nuclei.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is specific: the electrons in the outer shell are delocalised. The inner shells stay with their own nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Does boiling water break the covalent bonds in the molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. Boiling separates whole water molecules from one another. The covalent O-H bonds inside each molecule are not broken.
misconceptions.misconception: Water turns into steam, so the bonds holding the molecules together must have broken apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Change of state is described as particles separating, and the only bonds a student has drawn for water are the covalent ones, so those are the bonds assumed to break.
misconceptions.correction: Steam is still H2O. If the covalent bonds had broken, hydrogen and oxygen gas would be produced instead.

mcqs.stem: The specification describes covalent bonding in terms of which particles?

options.text: ions which have swapped electron pairs
options.rationale: Keeps the sharing language but attaches it to ions, which is the ionic case dressed up as covalent.

options.text: atoms sharing delocalised electrons
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of metallic bonding, chosen when the three types are not kept apart.

options.text: atoms which share pairs of electrons
options.rationale: This is the specification's wording: for covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons.

options.text: electrons moving from atom to atom
options.rationale: Describes the transfer step rather than any bond, and transfer belongs to ionic bonding.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a compound held together by ionic bonding?

options.text: lithium fluoride, a metal and a non-metal
options.rationale: Lithium is a metal and fluorine a non-metal, which is exactly the condition the specification gives for ionic bonding.

options.text: sulfur dioxide, a compound of two elements
options.rationale: Two different elements are present, but both are non-metals, so the bonding is covalent.

options.text: hydrogen chloride, a gas containing chloride
options.rationale: The -ide ending is read as proof of an ionic compound; hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals.

options.text: nitrogen gas, an element with very strong bonds
options.rationale: Strong bonding is present, but nitrogen is an element and its bonds are covalent.

mcqs.stem: Covalent bonding occurs in which of these?

options.text: compounds of non-metals only, never in elements
options.rationale: Correct about compounds but wrongly rules out elements such as chlorine and oxygen.

options.text: any compound made from two different elements
options.rationale: This is the test students misapply for ionic bonding, used here for covalent bonding instead.

options.text: non-metals combined with metals in a lattice
options.rationale: This describes ionic bonding, not covalent bonding.

options.text: most non-metallic elements and non-metal compounds
options.rationale: This is the specification statement: covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.

mcqs.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which type of bonding does it have?

options.text: ionic, because it contains two different elements
options.rationale: Two elements are present, but both are metals, so no ions of opposite charge form.

options.text: metallic, because alloys bond like pure metals
options.rationale: The specification states that metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.

options.text: ionic, since positive ions attract negative ions
options.rationale: The plus signs in a metal diagram are read as an ionic lattice; there are no negative ions in a metal.

options.text: covalent, as the atoms share outer electrons
options.rationale: Metal atoms do share electrons, but as delocalised electrons across the whole structure, not as pairs.

mcqs.stem: In terms of electrostatic forces, what is the ionic bond in sodium chloride?

options.text: attraction between oppositely charged ions
options.rationale: Chemical bonding is explained by electrostatic forces; in an ionic compound these act between the positive and negative ions.

options.text: the movement of an electron across the bond
options.rationale: Confuses the one-off transfer that creates the ions with the force that then holds them together.

options.text: a pair of electrons shared by the ions
options.rationale: Applies the covalent description to an ionic compound.

options.text: attraction between the two atomic nuclei
options.rationale: Both nuclei are positive and repel each other; the attraction is between the ions' opposite charges.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly links the three bond types to what happens to the outer electrons?

options.text: ionic and metallic share electrons; covalent transfers
options.rationale: Reverses which type transfers, a common slip when the three are learned as a list.

options.text: all three types involve sharing pairs of electrons
options.rationale: Applies the sharing description to ionic bonding, where electrons are transferred.

options.text: ionic transfers electrons; covalent and metallic share them
options.rationale: Ionic bonding transfers electrons, covalent bonding shares pairs between atoms and metallic bonding shares delocalised electrons.

options.text: covalent shares electrons; ionic and metallic do not
options.rationale: Denies that metal atoms share delocalised electrons, keeping electrons with their own atom.

mcqs.stem: A magnesium atom reacts with oxygen. What happens to magnesium's outer electrons?

options.text: six more are gained for a full outer shell
options.rationale: Takes the full outer shell rule literally instead of choosing the easier route of losing two.

options.text: they are lost, giving a 2- charged ion
options.rationale: Correct about the loss but reverses the sign; losing negative electrons leaves a positive ion.

options.text: they are shared with the oxygen atom
options.rationale: Applies covalent sharing to a reaction between a metal and a non-metal.

options.text: they are transferred, giving a 2+ ion
options.rationale: Metal atoms lose the electrons in their outer shell and become positively charged ions.

mcqs.stem: Which ions have the electronic structure of a noble gas?

options.text: none, since an ion keeps its structure
options.rationale: Treats electronic structure as fixed by the element, so no ion could match a noble gas.

options.text: those formed by Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
options.rationale: The specification names exactly these: ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.

options.text: only those whose charge equals the group
options.rationale: Uses the faulty group-number-equals-charge rule to decide which ions qualify.

options.text: only metal ions, since they lose electrons
options.rationale: Non-metal ions from Groups 6 and 7 also reach a noble gas structure, by gaining electrons.

mcqs.stem: A sodium atom, 2,8,1, forms a sodium ion. What is the ion's electronic structure and charge?

options.text: 2,8 with a charge of 1+, the same as neon
options.rationale: One outer electron is lost, leaving a full second shell and one more proton than electron.

options.text: 2,8,8 with a charge of 7-, like argon
options.rationale: Assumes sodium gains seven electrons to fill its outer shell rather than losing one.

options.text: 2,8,1 with a 1+ charge, shells unchanged
options.rationale: Keeps the atom's arrangement while adding the charge, so the electron is counted twice.

options.text: 2,8 but with a 1- charge, like neon
options.rationale: Gets the arrangement right but reverses the sign of the charge.

mcqs.stem: In a dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride, how is the sodium ion drawn?

options.text: in brackets with a 1+ charge and one outer electron
options.rationale: Draws the transferred electron twice, once on each ion.

options.text: with an arrow showing the electron crossing over
options.rationale: Treats the transfer arrow as the finished diagram rather than the pair of ions.

options.text: in brackets with a 1+ charge, outer shell empty
options.rationale: The transferred electron is drawn in the chlorine outer shell, so it is not drawn on sodium as well.

options.text: with one outer electron and no charge shown
options.rationale: This is the sodium atom, not the ion the diagram is meant to show.

mcqs.stem: Which dot and cross diagram represents magnesium chloride?

options.text: one Mg2+ ion drawn with a single Cl- ion
options.rationale: Pairs the ions one to one, as in sodium chloride, leaving the charges unbalanced.

options.text: one Mg2+ ion drawn with two Cl- ions
options.rationale: Magnesium loses two electrons, one to each chlorine atom, so the ratio is one to two.

options.text: two Mg2+ ions drawn with a Cl2- ion
options.rationale: Inverts the ratio and invents a 2- chloride ion from the group number.

options.text: one Mg2- ion next to two Cl+ ions
options.rationale: Reverses both signs, making the metal negative and the non-metal positive.

mcqs.stem: Which pairing of group and ionic charge is correct?

options.text: Group 6 forms an ion carrying a 6- charge
options.rationale: Takes the charge straight from the group number instead of the electrons needed.

options.text: Group 2 forms an ion with a charge of 2-
options.rationale: Right size of charge, wrong sign: a Group 2 metal loses electrons and becomes 2+.

options.text: Group 7 forms a 7+ ion, from its group number
options.rationale: Wrong in both size and sign; a Group 7 atom gains one electron to become 1-.

options.text: Group 6 forms an ion with a 2- charge
options.rationale: A Group 6 atom gains two electrons to reach a full outer shell, so the charge is 2-.

mcqs.stem: Calcium is in Group 2 and fluorine in Group 7. Which pair of ions do they form?

options.text: Ca2+ and F-, since calcium loses two
options.rationale: Group 2 metals lose two electrons to form 2+ ions; Group 7 non-metals gain one to form 1- ions.

options.text: Ca2+ and F7-, taken from the group numbers
options.rationale: Uses group number as the charge, which only works for Groups 1 and 2.

options.text: Ca2- and F+, as calcium gains electrons
options.rationale: Reverses the signs, making the metal the negative ion.

options.text: Ca2+ and F2-, so the formula is CaF
options.rationale: Adjusts the fluoride charge so the ions pair one to one.

mcqs.stem: Potassium is in Group 1 and oxygen in Group 6. What is the formula of the compound formed?

options.text: KO, because one ion of each is enough
options.rationale: Pairs the ions one to one without checking that the charges cancel.

options.text: K2O, as two 1+ ions balance one 2- ion
options.rationale: Potassium forms K+ and oxygen forms O2-, so two potassium ions are needed for each oxide ion.

options.text: K6O, read from the two group numbers
options.rationale: Reads the group numbers as the numbers of ions needed.

options.text: KO2, since oxygen forms two bonds
options.rationale: Applies a bonding count to an ionic formula and puts the subscript on the wrong element.

mcqs.stem: What holds an ionic compound together?

options.text: strong bonds pointing from each ion to its partner
options.rationale: Pictures the lattice as pairs joined by sticks rather than forces acting in all directions.

options.text: pairs of electrons shared between the ions
options.rationale: Applies covalent sharing to an ionic compound.

options.text: attraction between ions and loose electrons
options.rationale: Describes metallic bonding rather than ionic bonding.

options.text: strong electrostatic forces between charged ions
options.rationale: The specification states that ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

mcqs.stem: Why does the specification say that the forces in an ionic lattice act in all directions?

options.text: each ion is bonded to one partner ion only
options.rationale: Reads the formula NaCl as a molecule of two ions joined together.

options.text: the bonds point along fixed lines like sticks
options.rationale: Takes the sticks of a model as real, directional bonds.

options.text: each ion attracts all the ions around it
options.rationale: Electrostatic attraction is not confined to a line between two ions, so it holds the whole lattice together.

options.text: the ions only touch where the sticks join them
options.rationale: Treats a feature of the model as a feature of the substance.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows a regular cube of alternating small and large spheres, one element a metal. What is it?

options.text: separate molecules of the compound stacked up
options.rationale: Reads the repeating pattern as a stack of individual molecules.

options.text: a metal, as its atoms form a regular pattern
options.rationale: Uses regularity alone as the test, ignoring that two elements alternate and only one is a metal.

options.text: a giant covalent structure of shared pairs
options.rationale: Assumes any giant structure must be covalent, like silicon dioxide.

options.text: a giant ionic lattice with the ions alternating
options.rationale: A regular alternating array of two elements, one a metal, is the giant ionic structure of a compound such as sodium chloride.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a limitation of a ball and stick model of sodium chloride?

options.text: the sticks suggest gaps between the ions
options.rationale: In the real lattice the ions touch; the gaps and sticks exist only to make the arrangement visible.

options.text: it shows the compound as separate molecules
options.rationale: Ball and stick shows a continuous lattice, so this is not what the model gets wrong.

options.text: it shows forces in two directions only
options.rationale: This is a limitation of a flat two-dimensional diagram, not of a three-dimensional model.

options.text: it cannot show a regular arrangement
options.rationale: Showing the regular arrangement is exactly what a ball and stick model does well.

mcqs.stem: A model of an ionic compound shows 8 magnesium ions and 16 chloride ions. What is the empirical formula?

options.text: Mg8Cl16, the numbers counted in the model
options.rationale: Records the count rather than the ratio, which would change with the size of the model.

options.text: MgCl, since the ions pair up one to one
options.rationale: Forces a one to one ratio, as in sodium chloride.

options.text: MgCl2, the simplest whole number ratio
options.rationale: Eight to sixteen reduces to one to two, and an empirical formula is always the simplest ratio.

options.text: Mg2Cl, with the larger number first
options.rationale: Reverses the ratio, attaching the larger subscript to the wrong ion.

mcqs.stem: Water boils at 100 C. What does this tell you about the covalent bonds within a water molecule?

options.text: they are weak, since water boils easily
options.rationale: Uses the boiling point to judge the bonds inside the molecule.

options.text: nothing; the bonds in it are strong
options.rationale: Boiling separates whole molecules from each other. The bonds between atoms inside the molecule are strong and unaffected.

options.text: they break when the water turns to steam
options.rationale: Assumes a change of state breaks covalent bonds; steam is still H2O.

options.text: they are weaker than ionic bonds are
options.rationale: Compares the wrong pair of forces, again using melting and boiling points as the evidence.

mcqs.stem: Which of these substances consists of small molecules?

options.text: NaCl, a short two-symbol formula
options.rationale: Uses formula length as the test; sodium is a metal, so NaCl is a giant ionic structure.

options.text: SiO2, which looks just like CO2
options.rationale: The formulae match, but silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure.

options.text: CH4, a compound of two non-metals
options.rationale: Carbon and hydrogen are both non-metals, and methane is one of the small molecules named in the specification.

options.text: MgO, a compound made of two elements
options.rationale: Two elements are present, but magnesium is a metal, so magnesium oxide is ionic.

mcqs.stem: Poly(ethene) is a covalently bonded substance with very large molecules. What does that mean?

options.text: its molecules are very large but separate
options.rationale: A polymer consists of very large molecules; each chain is a separate molecule.

options.text: it has a giant covalent structure like diamond
options.rationale: Treats a very large molecule and a giant structure as the same thing.

options.text: the covalent bonds in it must be weaker
options.rationale: Uses the fact that polymers soften on heating to judge the covalent bonds.

options.text: it is a mixture of very many small molecules
options.rationale: The small molecules have joined into chains; they are no longer separate.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of substances both have giant covalent structures?

options.text: carbon dioxide and silicon dioxide, two oxides
options.rationale: The similar formulae hide the fact that carbon dioxide is a small molecule.

options.text: diamond and silicon dioxide, the named examples
options.rationale: These are the two giant covalent structures given in the specification.

options.text: poly(ethene) and diamond, both very large
options.rationale: Poly(ethene) has very large molecules, not a giant covalent structure.

options.text: sodium chloride and diamond, both giant
options.rationale: Sodium chloride is giant, but the bonding is ionic, not covalent.

mcqs.stem: In the representation of a polymer, what does n stand for?

options.text: a number you work out from the diagram
options.rationale: Treats n as an unknown to be calculated, like a subscript in a formula.

options.text: the count of carbon atoms in the unit
options.rationale: Attaches n to something countable in the drawing.

options.text: the simplest whole number ratio of atoms
options.rationale: Confuses n with the rule for writing an empirical formula.

options.text: a large number of repeating units
options.rationale: The specification states only that n is a large number.

mcqs.stem: How many shared pairs of electrons are there between the atoms in an oxygen molecule, O2?

options.text: two, drawn as four electrons in the overlap
options.rationale: Each oxygen atom needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared: a double bond.

options.text: one, since a covalent bond is one shared pair
options.rationale: Applies the hydrogen molecule case, where one pair is all that is needed.

options.text: four, one for each electron in the overlap
options.rationale: Counts individual electrons rather than pairs.

options.text: six, since each atom has six outer electrons
options.rationale: Counts the outer electrons of one atom rather than the electrons shared.

mcqs.stem: In the displayed formula of methane, what does each of the four lines represent?

options.text: one electron passed from carbon to hydrogen
options.rationale: Reads the line as a single electron, and as transferred rather than shared.

options.text: the two electrons carbon contributes
options.rationale: Counts the contributed electrons separately instead of counting the pair as one bond.

options.text: a stick that holds the two atoms apart
options.rationale: Takes the model's stick literally as a physical connector.

options.text: one single bond, that is one shared pair
options.rationale: A line is used to represent a single covalent bond, which is one shared pair of electrons.

mcqs.stem: What is a limitation of a two-dimensional displayed formula of a methane molecule?

options.text: it shows the atoms at their true relative size
options.rationale: A displayed formula shows no sizes at all, so this is not what it gets wrong.

options.text: it gives the ratio of atoms, not the number
options.rationale: A displayed formula shows every atom, so it gives the molecular formula.

options.text: it does not show the real shape of the molecule
options.rationale: A flat drawing cannot show that the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

options.text: it hides how strong the bonds actually are
options.rationale: Bond strength is not shown by any diagram, and is not the limitation being asked about.

mcqs.stem: A model of ethene shows two black balls (carbon), four white balls (hydrogen) and six sticks. What is the molecular formula?

options.text: CH2, the simplest whole number ratio
options.rationale: Simplifies a molecular formula as though it were an empirical formula.

options.text: C2H4, counting only the balls
options.rationale: The molecular formula counts the atoms shown: two carbon and four hydrogen.

options.text: C2H6, one hydrogen for each stick
options.rationale: Counts the sticks instead of the balls, giving six hydrogen atoms.

options.text: C6H4, taking the sticks as carbons
options.rationale: Counts the sticks as atoms of the other element in the model.

mcqs.stem: How are the atoms arranged in a pure metal?

options.text: in a giant structure with a regular pattern
options.rationale: The specification states that metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.

options.text: randomly, in a closely packed jumble of atoms
options.rationale: Extends the free movement of the delocalised electrons to the atoms themselves.

options.text: a lattice of positive and negative ions
options.rationale: Reads the plus signs in a metal diagram as an ionic lattice.

options.text: in small groups of a few joined atoms
options.rationale: Treats a metal as made of molecules, as a covalent element would be.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the electrons in a metal is correct?

options.text: each atom keeps its outer electrons, loosely
options.rationale: Keeps the shell picture, in which every electron belongs to one atom.

options.text: every electron in every atom is delocalised
options.rationale: Extends delocalisation to the inner shells, which stay with their own nucleus.

options.text: the outer electrons are free to move about
options.rationale: The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure.

options.text: the electrons are transferred to the ions
options.rationale: Describes ionic bonding; in a metal nothing accepts the electrons.
